  3. InvoiceZero — Watermark-free multi-currency Invoice & Quotation generator (USDT, USD, CNY, EUR, GBP, USDC) with auto tax/discount math, JSON backup/restore, and crisp A4 PDF export.
  4. ResumeMD Zero — Local Markdown resume builder with 3 ATS-friendly themes and one-click A4 PDF print export.
  5. ChainCalc Zero — Client-side DeFi Impermanent Loss (Uniswap V2/V3), Gas-Adjusted APY compounding, and Position Sizing calculator.
  6. XiaheAI Hub — Bilingual portal bringing all tools together (plus source links and custom automation inquiries).

3 Modern Browser Primitives That Replaced 500 KB of Dependencies

1. Native Instead of Modal Libraries

Modern HTML

handles focus trapping, Esc dismissal, and ::backdrop styling natively:

 id="tipDialog">
  
Support Open-Source Maintenance

Sensitive drafts (client invoices, resumes) stay strictly in localStorage and can be exported/imported as portable .json files — no database costs, no GDPR liability, and zero latency.

title: I built a Modbus simulator that Claude drives over MCP: test SCADA without a PLC
summary:
Disclosure: I work on fieldpuppet, the open-source simulator in this post. It is maintained by the team behind PLCGateway.

Here is a prompt I can now type into Claude:

Set up 50 energy meters starting at port 6000. Make meter 12 stop answering for 30 seconds, then tell me which registers my SCADA read from it.

A few seconds later there are 50 Modbus TCP devices listening on my laptop, one of them goes silent on schedule, and I get a report of what my software polled. No PLC, no meter, no cabinet.

This post explains why I built it, how the MCP part works, and how to use it without any AI at all.

The problem: the hardware is never on your desk

If you write software that talks Modbus TCP (a SCADA screen, a gateway, a historian, a data collector), you know this situation. The code is ready, but the PLC is in a cabinet at the customer site, the energy meter has not shipped yet, and nobody will let you unplug a pump just to see how your software handles a timeout.

A register table that returns fixed numbers does not help much. Real testing needs:

  • Many devices at once, because polling 1 device and polling 200 behave very differently.
  • Values that move, so trends, alarms and scaling can be checked.
  • Faults on demand: slow answers, no answer, exception replies, dropped connections. These break software in the field and are the hardest to reproduce with real equipment.
  • A record of what your software asked for, so you can see whether it polls the registers you think it does.

Why MCP fits this job

Setting up test devices is boring, repetitive work: copy a register list from a manual, pick ports, write a fault timeline. It is exactly the kind of work an assistant does well if it has the right tools.

fieldpuppet is a single Rust executable of about 2 MB with an MCP server built in. It exposes 22 tools, such as create_device, set_signal, apply_scenario, inject_fault and get_traffic_log. Every tool carries read-only and destructive hints, so the client knows which calls change state.

For Claude Code it is one line:

claude mcp add fieldpuppet -- /full/path/to/fieldpuppet mcp

For Claude Desktop, each release has an .mcpb bundle you can install from the Extensions settings. Any MCP client that can start a local server over stdio works.

Things I ask it most often:

  • "Here is the register list from a device manual. Build a simulated device that matches it."
  • "Make the tank level rise from 20 % to 95 % over two minutes, then switch the high level alarm on."
  • "Pump 2 should answer with a device busy exception for the next 30 seconds."
  • "Which registers has my SCADA been reading from the drive in the last minute?"

A read-only web dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:5080 shows every device, its live values and a feed of everything the assistant changed, so you are never guessing what it did.

It works without AI too

Describe the devices in YAML:

devices:
  - id: pump-1
    template: pump
    port: 5020

  - id: dosing-skid
    port: 5021
    points:
      - name: chlorine_ppm
        table: input
        address: 0
        scale: 0.01
        unit: ppm
        value: 0.8
        signal: { type: random_walk, min: 0.5, max: 1.2, step: 0.02 }

Run it:

fieldpuppet run water-station.yaml

Point your own software at 127.0.0.1, port 5020 or 5021, unit id 1. The chlorine value drifts between 0.5 and 1.2 ppm like a real sensor would. Addresses are zero-based protocol addresses, so holding register 40001 is address 0.

Test the bad days, not only the good ones

Four fault types are available, each with an optional time limit:

  • delay: correct answers, but late
  • no_response: your client sees a timeout
  • exception: a Modbus exception such as device busy
  • disconnect: the connection closes on every request

This is how you find out whether your software reconnects, whether one dead device stalls the polling of the other 49, and whether stale values are marked as stale.

Limits

  • Modbus TCP only. No serial RTU or ASCII yet.
  • Devices do not model process behaviour. A pump does not stop because its run coil was cleared; a scenario or the assistant has to change the values.
  • Simulation only. It answers requests sent to it and never connects to real equipment.

Try it

The code is on GitHub under MIT / Apache 2.0: CybriantOps/fieldpuppet. It is a new project, so bug reports and feature requests are very welcome.

Which fault case has caused you the most trouble in the field?

title: What If Online Proctors Could Tell the Difference Between a Panic Attack and Cheating? Meet AegisPulse.
summary:
Imagine this: You're halfway through a high-stakes exam that determines your university scholarship.

Your chest tightens. Your heart rate shoots through the roof. Your breathing turns shallow and rapid. You look frantically around your screen, trying to steady your racing thoughts.

Seconds later, a terrifying red box flashes:
🚨 SUSPICIOUS BIOMETRIC ANOMALY. EXAM TERMINATED FOR DISHONESTY.

You weren't cheating. You were having an acute panic attack. But today’s remote proctoring algorithms can’t tell the difference between a student suffocating under test anxiety and someone peeking at an answer key.

Every year, over 80 million students take exams online, and thousands of neurodivergent or anxious students face disciplinary hearings simply for having a nervous system. Meanwhile, actual cheaters with hidden phones slip right past basic face-detection software.

I built AegisPulse to fix this broken, punitive paradigm—turning proctoring into an ethical, privacy-preserving guardian powered by contactless physiological sensing.

What I Built

AegisPulse is the first ethical exam integrity and well-being platform that separates test anxiety from academic dishonesty in real time—completely on-device, with zero video or audio ever leaving the candidate's browser.

Instead of treating students like suspects in an interrogation room, AegisPulse acts like a compassionate proctor:

🫀 Contactless Biometric Baseline: In the first 5 seconds, it establishes your personal resting heart rate and respiratory baseline using contactless camera sensing.
🛡️ The Protected Panic Shield: If your heart surges to 138 BPM and your breathing spikes, but your eyes remain locked on the test paper, AegisPulse recognizes an acute anxiety episode. It automatically pauses the exam clock, suppresses false cheating penalties, and launches an interactive 4-7-8 resonant box-breathing reset.

pitch) and covert whispers, the system decomposes the anomaly in an Explainable AI forensic matrix.

The entire project is open-source, fully typed in TypeScript and Python, and designed to run entirely client-side:

GitHub repository- https://github.com/yuvanshankarm007/aegispulse
How It Responds to Human Signals

The real magic of AegisPulse lives in how it fuses the Presage SmartSpectra SDK with client-side computer vision:

We pipe four live physiological data streams over a local WebSocket bridge (ws://127.0.0.1:8765/smartspectra):

Cardiac Pulse (BPM) — Sub-surface facial chrominance rPPG.
Respiration Rate (RPM) — Subtle chest and nasal optical motion flow.
Heart Rate Variability (HRV RMSSD) — Autonomic nervous system vagal tone.
Signal Quality Index (SQI %) — Telemetry confidence scoring.

When anxiety strikes, the candidate’s physiology goes wild, but their gaze stays centered on the test. AegisPulse rewards that focus by pausing the clock and opening a gentle, harmonic box-breathing circle to help them regain composure.

Conversely, when someone looks down at a phone under their desk, their heart rate stays normal, but their gaze vector plunges
and our 36-band acoustic FFT spectrogram isolates covert speech frequencies (300−3400Hz).

It's fair, explainable, and grounded in real human physiology.

Prize Categories
🌟 Best Thoughtful Real-World Use

Online exams shouldn't feel like a police state. Millions of students struggle with anxiety disorders, neurodivergence, or high-stress panic. AegisPulse is built specifically to protect them:

Calibrated to the individual: It doesn't rely on arbitrary global thresholds; it personalizes baselines in 5 seconds.
Dignity first: When a student is overwhelmed, it pauses the exam and guides them back to calm without academic penalty.
Human in the loop: Proctors can grant extra time or send reassuring messages directly through a dual-tab BroadcastChannel.
🎨 Most Creative or Delightful Use

Proctoring is universally despised for being invasive and cold. AegisPulse flips the entire experience into something genuinely delightful:

Smooth in-browser 5-point reticle calibration that maps your unique cranial anatomy in seconds.
A soothing, resonant 4-7-8 breathing circle that synchronizes with your heartbeat.
A standalone verification portal where admissions officers can run an interactive "1-Byte Tamper Test" to watch cryptographic signatures break in real time!
Consent and Data Handling

We took an uncompromising stance on student privacy: Zero Data Retention (ZDR).

Clear, Opt-In Onboarding: The test cannot begin without the candidate explicitly reviewing and accepting the biometric consent gate.
100% On-Device & Ephemeral: Raw video frames and microphone streams are processed exclusively in browser memory. Not a single frame or audio buffer is ever written to disk or sent over the internet.
No Biometric Storage: The system never creates facial recognition vectors, biometrics IDs, or face templates.
Wellness, Not Diagnostics: AegisPulse is designed purely as an educational wellness and exam integrity aid; it makes zero medical claims or clinical diagnoses.
Cryptographic Proofs Over Surveillance: Instead of saving hours of student video recordings, universities receive an anonymized cryptographic JSON certificate signed with ECDSA P-256, mathematically proving the test was taken legitimately without storing the student's personal data.

title: epub_rtl: a pure-Flutter EPUB parser and reader for right-to-left books
summary:
An EPUB file is a zip archive of XHTML chapters with a manifest, a reading order and a table of contents. For an Arabic book, a reader has more to get right than opening the zip. The book declares that its pages progress from right to left, and the reader has to swipe the other way. A paragraph mixes Arabic with an English word or a number, and the bidi algorithm needs the right isolates to keep the sentence in order. The table of contents should open from the right side. The body text needs an Arabic font.

On the Flutter side, the README notes the state of the usual packages: epubx has had no release since June 2023, and epub_view depends on it and on the archived scrollable_positioned_list.

epub_rtl is a pure-Flutter EPUB 2/3 parser and reader that handles right-to-left books. It is built for Arabic and other RTL texts, and it uses no WebView.

What it does

The package has three layers. You can use the parser alone, the parser with the content model, or all three.

The parser

It is pure Dart and depends only on archive and xml.

  • It finds the package document through META-INF/container.xml, then reads the OPF: metadata (titles, creators with role and file-as, languages, identifiers, publisher, date, description, dcterms:modified and the cover image), the manifest, and the spine with linear and page-progression-direction.
  • EpubBook.isRtl uses the spine direction, and falls back to the book language when the spine declares none.
  • For navigation, it reads the EPUB 3 nav document (toc, landmarks, page-list), and falls back to the EPUB 2 NCX with the guide element as landmarks.
  • Content is read by href, with relative paths, percent-encoding and fragments resolved.
  • Reading is lazy. Only the zip directory is read up front. Each chapter or resource is inflated when it is requested, and it is not cached. EpubBook.openFile reads entries from disk on demand.

Malformed books throw a typed EpubException with an EpubErrorKind. With lenient: true, the parser recovers from common real-world errors and records them in warnings: a missing or misplaced mimetype, a missing NCX or nav document, missing or unknown media types, dangling spine references and wrong letter case in paths.

A book with DRM listed in META-INF/encryption.xml is refused with EpubErrorKind.encrypted. A book whose only encrypted resources are obfuscated fonts opens in lenient mode, and those fonts are unreadable.

The content model

EpubChapter turns a chapter's XHTML into a flat list of blocks. Each id maps to a block index, which is what locations point to.

  • Blocks: headings, paragraphs, pre, images (including SVG-wrapped covers), lists, blockquotes, basic tables and rules.
  • Inline content: emphasis, bold, underline, strike, sup/sub, code, links and basic ruby.
  • dir and lang are inherited, and dir="auto" uses the first strong character.
  • Inline dir is wrapped in bidi isolates (LRI/RLI … PDI), bdi in FSI … PDI, and bdo in LRO/RLO … PDF.
  • A CSS subset is read from linked stylesheets, style elements and style attributes: text-align, font-style, font-weight, margins, text-indent, direction and display: none, with tag, class, id and descendant selectors.

The reader

EpubReaderView is a Flutter widget with two modes. scroll is one continuous vertical scroll through the whole book. paginated shows one chapter per page, swiped in the book's reading direction, so RTL books advance with a right swipe.

The reading position is an EpubLocation: spine index, element index and an offset fraction. You can serialise it with toJson or encode, restore it with initialLocation, and follow it through onLocationChanged and the controller.

EpubReaderController has jumpTo, jumpToHref (for TOC entries and internal links), nextChapter and previousChapter. EpubTocDrawer is a table-of-contents drawer laid out in the book's direction.

EpubReaderSettings covers font size and line height, light, sepia and dark themes, justification, and arabicFontFamily, which is used for RTL-language runs and placed first in the fallback list.

Internal links jump inside the book, and external links go to your onExternalLink callback. Jumps inside a chapter use GlobalKeys and Scrollable.ensureVisible, so the package does not depend on scrollable_positioned_list.

How to use it

Add it from GitHub:

dependencies:
  epub_rtl:
    git: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/epub_rtl

It needs Flutter 3.24 or later. A complete reader screen, from the README:

import 'package:epub_rtl/epub_rtl.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class ReaderScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const ReaderScreen({super.key, required this.bytes, this.saved});

  final List<int> bytes;
  final String? saved; // a previously stored EpubLocation.encode()

  @override
  State<ReaderScreen> createState() => _ReaderScreenState();
}

class _ReaderScreenState extends State<ReaderScreen> {
  late final EpubBook book = EpubBook.fromBytes(widget.bytes, lenient: true);
  final controller = EpubReaderController();

  @override
  void dispose() {
    controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: Text(book.metadata.title)),
        drawer: EpubTocDrawer(book: book, controller: controller),
        body: EpubReaderView(
          book: book,
          controller: controller,
          mode: EpubReaderMode.paginated,
          settings: const EpubReaderSettings(
            fontSize: 20,
            theme: EpubReaderTheme.sepia,
            arabicFontFamily: 'Amiri', // bundle the font in your app
            justify: true,
          ),
          initialLocation:
              widget.saved == null ? null : EpubLocation.tryDecode(widget.saved!),
          onLocationChanged: (location) {
            // Persist location.encode() or location.toJson().
          },
          onExternalLink: (url) {
            // Open with url_launcher, for example.
          },
        ),
      );
}

If you only need the parser:

final book = EpubBook.fromBytes(bytes);
print(book.metadata.title);
print(book.spine.pageProgressionDirection); // PageProgressionDirection.rtl
for (final entry in book.navigation.toc) {
  print('${entry.title} -> ${entry.href}');
}
final chapter = EpubChapter.fromBook(book, 0);
print(chapter.blocks.length);

Coming from epubx or epub_view

The README has a mapping table. The main lines: EpubReader.readBook(bytes), which is async and loads everything, becomes EpubBook.fromBytes(bytes), which is sync and lazy. book.Title becomes book.metadata.title. chapter.HtmlContent becomes book.chapterHtml(i) or EpubChapter.fromBook(book, i). EpubView with its EpubController becomes EpubReaderView with an EpubReaderController, and EpubViewTableOfContents becomes EpubTocDrawer.

One thing does not carry over: locations are not EPUB CFIs. Saved epub_view CFIs cannot be converted.

Things to know

  • DRM-encrypted books are refused. Obfuscated embedded fonts are not de-obfuscated, and embedded fonts are not loaded. Use fontFamily and arabicFontFamily with fonts bundled in your app.
  • Paginated mode is one chapter per page. The page scrolls vertically. The text is not split into screen-sized pages.
  • The CSS support is a small subset. No floats, positioning, colours, font sizes from CSS, pseudo-classes, >/+/~ selectors or @media rules.
  • Tables are basic: no colspan or rowspan. Ruby is shown as annotation-over-base, without full ruby layout.
  • Not rendered: SVG images, audio, video, MathML and scripts. Fixed-layout EPUBs are rendered as reflowable text.
  • Long chapters cost more. Each chapter is built as one widget subtree so that element keys exist for jumps. Very long single chapters cost more to lay out.
  • Web. EpubBook.openFile needs dart:io and is not available on the web. Use fromBytes there.
  • Test data. No third-party book content is bundled. The test fixtures and the example's sample book are generated in code, with text written for the package.

Why I built it

The README states the problem in two sentences: the existing parser has had no release since June 2023, and the existing viewer depends on it and on an archived scrolling package.

For an Arabic book, direction is not a setting you add at the end. It decides which way a swipe goes, which side the drawer opens from, how a mixed Arabic and Latin sentence is isolated, and which font the text falls back to. So I wrote the reader with direction read from the book itself, from the spine first and the language second, and applied at every level: the page view, the drawer, the paragraph and the inline run. Doing it with Flutter widgets instead of a WebView keeps the whole thing in one rendering system, with a reading position that can be saved as a small string and restored.

Get the code

The source, the migration table, an example app with a generated sample book and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/epub_rtl. It is MIT licensed.

title: I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem
summary:
I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud Ampere A1's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem

Getting an Oracle Cloud Ampere A1 instance can be frustrating.

You may have your OCI account configured, your network ready, your quotas checked, and your VM configuration prepared — but capacity availability can still get in the way.

I wanted a simpler way to handle this workflow.

So I started building a Python automation tool for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). What began as a personal automation script gradually evolved into a cross-platform CLI with interactive configuration, installation scripts, monitoring capabilities, safety checks, and support for AI coding agents.

!OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

Today, I'm sharing it with the developer community.

GitHub: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Working with OCI A1 instances involves more than just clicking the Create Instance button.

Before attempting to launch an instance, there are several things worth checking:

Is A1 capacity currently available in my region and availability domain?
Are my OCPU and memory quotas sufficient?
Is my existing VCN and subnet configuration valid?
Is the selected image appropriate?
Am I staying within my intended compute and storage budget?
How can I monitor capacity without repeatedly doing the same manual checks?

I didn't want to build another cloud dashboard or a complicated infrastructure platform.

I wanted a lightweight tool that could automate repetitive checks and provide a manageable workflow from the terminal.

What I Built
OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

A Python-based CLI designed to help OCI users inspect their environment, check A1 capacity, validate configuration, and optionally request one VM through an explicitly guarded workflow.

The project supports Windows and Linux.

What It Can Do

  1. A1 Capacity Monitoring

Check OCI A1 availability and monitor capacity using configurable retry and backoff behavior.

  1. Quota and Configuration Checks

Validate important settings such as:

Home region and availability domain.
Existing VCN and public subnet.
Compute and storage limits.
A1 instance configuration.
Image and SSH public-key settings.
Existing instances and resource usage.

  1. Interactive Terminal Interface

Instead of remembering every command, users can open the application and navigate through an interactive terminal menu.

  1. Guided Configuration

The configuration editor allows users to work through settings in organized groups, validate values, review changes, and save safely.

  1. Windows and Linux Installers

The project includes PowerShell and shell installers that create an isolated Python environment and initialize a safe starter configuration.

  1. AI Coding-Agent Support

The repository includes instructions and project memory for tools such as:

Claude Code
OpenAI Codex
Gemini CLI
GitHub Copilot
Other agentic development environments

The idea is to make it easier to understand, maintain, and extend the project with AI assistance.

Some Implementation Decisions I Found Interesting

This project was also a useful exercise in making an existing automation tool more reusable.

A few decisions shaped the architecture.

Keeping the Existing Engine

Rather than rewriting the original automation logic, I introduced a new oci-platform CLI layer around the existing Python engine.

This allowed me to preserve existing functionality while improving how users interact with it.

Handling Windows and Linux Differences

One portability issue came from using the POSIX-only fcntl module for process locking.

That approach wasn't suitable for Windows.

I replaced the unconditional platform-specific import with a cross-platform locking implementation.

It was a good reminder that cross-platform support needs to be considered at the application level, not just in the installer.

Making Configuration Safer

I didn't want setup to accidentally arm VM creation or overwrite an existing installation.

The installers refuse to overwrite an existing target directory, and the configuration workflow keeps VM creation disabled.

These are deliberate design decisions, not just documentation warnings.

Safety Is a Core Part of the Design

Because this application interacts with cloud infrastructure, I wanted the default behavior to be read-only.

VM creation requires three independent safeguards:

mode.creation_enabled=true in the local configuration.
The exact confirmation phrase LAUNCH_ONE_ALWAYS_FREE_INSTANCE.
The CLI flag --enable-create.

An actual launch also requires the operator's explicit authorization.

The application is designed around an existing network rather than automatically creating or modifying networking resources.

It does not upgrade OCI accounts, terminate existing instances, or promise guaranteed capacity or zero billing.

A capacity check is not a reservation, and Always Free eligibility must always be verified against your own OCI account and current Oracle terms.

Development and Testing

I wanted to validate more than just whether the Python code worked on my own machine.

The repository now has GitHub Actions workflows covering:

Python 3.11 and 3.12.
Windows and Ubuntu.
Application compilation and unit tests.
CLI startup and packaging.
Installer safety checks.
A fresh Linux installer integration test.

The Linux integration test checks installation in a clean temporary directory, verifies the installed commit, confirms the starter configuration keeps creation disabled, and checks that existing directories are preserved.

I also encountered an environment-related problem while trying to run a Linux installation test in an isolated Debian container: DNS resolution for raw.githubusercontent.com failed.

Instead of marking that attempt as successful, I added hosted Ubuntu integration coverage to the CI workflow.

The latest main commit passed all six CI jobs.

I also tested a fresh Windows installation and the interactive CLI on a second PC; that result was reported by the operator.

There is still work to do around live OCI validation, so I am not claiming that every real-world tenancy or capacity scenario has been verified.

Getting Started

You need:

Git
Python 3.11 or newer
Windows (PowerShell)

Download the installer:

powershell
Invoke-WebRequest "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.ps1" -OutFile install.ps1

Review the installer:

powershell
Get-Content .\install.ps1

Run the installer:

powershell
.\install.ps1

Linux

Download the installer:

bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.sh

Review the installer:

bash
less install.sh

Run the installer:

bash
bash install.sh

Launch the Interactive CLI

Windows:

powershell
$cli = "$HOME\oci-automation-platform.venv\Scripts\oci-platform.exe"
& $cli

Linux:

bash
CLI="$HOME/oci-automation-platform/.venv/bin/oci-platform"
"$CLI"

Start with local configuration and diagnostics before connecting to your OCI environment.

The installer creates a starter configuration with VM creation disabled. Follow the detailed instructions in the repository before running live OCI checks.

What's Next?

The initial V1 code-delivery milestone is complete, but I see this as the beginning of community testing rather than the end of development.

Some areas I'd like to improve through feedback:

More real-world OCI A1 edge-case testing.
Better diagnostics and operator feedback.
Additional installation and configuration testing across environments.
Improvements to monitoring and retry behavior.
More useful workflows for AI-assisted maintenance.

I also want to keep the project lightweight rather than turn it into a large platform with unnecessary services.

I'd Love Your Feedback

I'm especially interested in hearing from developers who use Oracle Cloud, Python automation, or cross-platform CLI tools.

A few questions:

Would you find a tool like this useful for managing OCI A1 capacity?
What edge cases should I test before a wider release?
Is the interactive terminal experience a good approach, or would you prefer a different workflow?
What would you improve in the current architecture?

Feedback, bug reports, and contributions are welcome.

Explore the Project

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

Thanks for reading!

A Python-based CLI designed to help OCI users inspect their environment, check A1 capacity, validate configuration, and optionally request one VM through an explicitly guarded workflow.

The project supports Windows and Linux.

What It Can Do

  1. A1 Capacity Monitoring

Check OCI A1 availability and monitor capacity using configurable retry and backoff behavior.

  1. Quota and Configuration Checks

Validate important settings such as:

Home region and availability domain.
Existing VCN and public subnet.
Compute and storage limits.
A1 instance configuration.
Image and SSH public-key settings.
Existing instances and resource usage.

  1. Interactive Terminal Interface

Instead of remembering every command, users can open the application and navigate through an interactive terminal menu.

  1. Guided Configuration

The configuration editor allows users to work through settings in organized groups, validate values, review changes, and save safely.

  1. Windows and Linux Installers

The project includes PowerShell and shell installers that create an isolated Python environment and initialize a safe starter configuration.

  1. AI Coding-Agent Support

The repository includes instructions and project memory for tools such as:

Claude Code
OpenAI Codex
Gemini CLI
GitHub Copilot
Other agentic development environments

The idea is to make it easier to understand, maintain, and extend the project with AI assistance.

Some Implementation Decisions I Found Interesting

This project was also a useful exercise in making an existing automation tool more reusable.

A few decisions shaped the architecture.

Keeping the Existing Engine

Rather than rewriting the original automation logic, I introduced a new oci-platform CLI layer around the existing Python engine.

This allowed me to preserve existing functionality while improving how users interact with it.

Handling Windows and Linux Differences

One portability issue came from using the POSIX-only fcntl module for process locking.

That approach wasn't suitable for Windows.

I replaced the unconditional platform-specific import with a cross-platform locking implementation.

It was a good reminder that cross-platform support needs to be considered at the application level, not just in the installer.

Making Configuration Safer

I didn't want setup to accidentally arm VM creation or overwrite an existing installation.

The installers refuse to overwrite an existing target directory, and the configuration workflow keeps VM creation disabled.

These are deliberate design decisions, not just documentation warnings.

Safety Is a Core Part of the Design

Because this application interacts with cloud infrastructure, I wanted the default behavior to be read-only.

VM creation requires three independent safeguards:

mode.creation_enabled=true in the local configuration.
The exact confirmation phrase LAUNCH_ONE_ALWAYS_FREE_INSTANCE.
The CLI flag --enable-create.

An actual launch also requires the operator's explicit authorization.

The application is designed around an existing network rather than automatically creating or modifying networking resources.

It does not upgrade OCI accounts, terminate existing instances, or promise guaranteed capacity or zero billing.

A capacity check is not a reservation, and Always Free eligibility must always be verified against your own OCI account and current Oracle terms.

Development and Testing

I wanted to validate more than just whether the Python code worked on my own machine.

The repository now has GitHub Actions workflows covering:

Python 3.11 and 3.12.
Windows and Ubuntu.
Application compilation and unit tests.
CLI startup and packaging.
Installer safety checks.
A fresh Linux installer integration test.

The Linux integration test checks installation in a clean temporary directory, verifies the installed commit, confirms the starter configuration keeps creation disabled, and checks that existing directories are preserved.

I also encountered an environment-related problem while trying to run a Linux installation test in an isolated Debian container: DNS resolution for raw.githubusercontent.com failed.

Instead of marking that attempt as successful, I added hosted Ubuntu integration coverage to the CI workflow.

The latest main commit passed all six CI jobs.

I also tested a fresh Windows installation and the interactive CLI on a second PC; that result was reported by the operator.

There is still work to do around live OCI validation, so I am not claiming that every real-world tenancy or capacity scenario has been verified.

Getting Started

You need:

Git
Python 3.11 or newer
Windows (PowerShell)

Download the installer:

powershell
Invoke-WebRequest "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.ps1" -OutFile install.ps1

Review the installer:

powershell
Get-Content .\install.ps1

Run the installer:

powershell
.\install.ps1

Linux

Download the installer:

bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.sh

Review the installer:

bash
less install.sh

Run the installer:

bash
bash install.sh

Launch the Interactive CLI

Windows:

powershell
$cli = "$HOME\oci-automation-platform.venv\Scripts\oci-platform.exe"
& $cli

Linux:

bash
CLI="$HOME/oci-automation-platform/.venv/bin/oci-platform"
"$CLI"

Start with local configuration and diagnostics before connecting to your OCI environment.

The installer creates a starter configuration with VM creation disabled. Follow the detailed instructions in the repository before running live OCI checks.

What's Next?

The initial V1 code-delivery milestone is complete, but I see this as the beginning of community testing rather than the end of development.

Some areas I'd like to improve through feedback:

More real-world OCI A1 edge-case testing.
Better diagnostics and operator feedback.
Additional installation and configuration testing across environments.
Improvements to monitoring and retry behavior.
More useful workflows for AI-assisted maintenance.

I also want to keep the project lightweight rather than turn it into a large platform with unnecessary services.

I'd Love Your Feedback

I'm especially interested in hearing from developers who use Oracle Cloud, Python automation, or cross-platform CLI tools.

A few questions:

Would you find a tool like this useful for managing OCI A1 capacity?
What edge cases should I test before a wider release?
Is the interactive terminal experience a good approach, or would you prefer a different workflow?
What would you improve in the current architecture?

Feedback, bug reports, and contributions are welcome.

Explore the Project

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

Thanks for reading!

title: Where Open-Source Tools Quietly Fail: The Authentication Chain
summary:
Where Open-Source Tools Quietly Fail: The Authentication Chain

Database security writing loves the database: accounts, grants, encryption at rest. I spend my weeks auditing a different layer — the open-source tools that sit next to the database. Admin consoles, BI panels, backup agents, report engines. The tools that hold production credentials and whose CVEs keep tracing back not to the login form itself, but to the chain behind it.

The useful mental model is to stop treating "authentication" as a feature and start treating it as a chain of five links. Every component I've audited fails at exactly one of them — and only one of them is the password check.

Link 1: The login form

Everyone tests the login form. The failures here are quieter than SQL injection:

  • Default accounts that survive upgrades. The installer creates admin, the upgrade script doesn't remove it, and the docs never mention it. Check the migration scripts, not just the docs.
  • Password comparison in code. Somewhere between the form and the database, a comparison happens. When it's a string equality on a fetched hash instead of a constant-time verify on a computed one, you have a timing oracle — and more commonly, a hashing scheme chosen in 2015 that nobody revisited.

Link 2: The token

The login succeeds and the component mints a token. This is where I find the most per-issue impact:

  • JWT secrets committed to source. Still, in 2026. Grep the repository for signing keys before reading anything else.
  • alg confusion. The library accepts more algorithms than the code intends. Rare in mature projects, endemic in young ones.
  • Sessions that never expire because expiry is a config key nobody sets. The default value is zero, zero means "no expiry," and no test catches this because tests log in and log out.

Link 3: The remember-me cookie

Remember-me is a serialization feature disguised as a convenience feature. State goes into a cookie, the server trusts the cookie later. When the "state" is a serialized object graph, you're one gadget chain away from a much worse CVE than "session forgery." When it's a signed user ID, check what signs it — I've found remember-me cookies signed with the same key as the JWT, which means forging one forges the other.

Link 4: The password reset flow

The reset flow is the authentication chain running without a password, which makes it the most security-critical code in the component and, consistently, the least reviewed:

  • Reset tokens that double as session tokens. The token resets the password and then logs you in. Now the token's lifetime is the session's lifetime, and the token was sent over email.
  • Host header injection in the reset email. The link in the email is built from the request's Host header. An attacker who can get a request to the server with a chosen Host header sends the victim a poisoned reset link. It's a one-line bug that keeps being shipped.

Link 5: The service account

The last link is the one no user ever sees: the API key the component uses for its own operations, and the ones it issues for integrations. Shared by all users, no expiry, and in several published cases, one of them authenticates as admin. When you audit, list every key type — user keys, integration keys, internal keys — and check the middleware that validates them. The gap between "valid key" and "this key may do this" is where the whole chain collapses.

The chain-shaped audit

Read the chain in order, and do it from source:

  1. Find the login handler. Read the comparison.
  2. Find the token mint. Find the expiry check. Grep for the signing key.
  3. Find the remember-me serializer. Check what it trusts and what signs it.
  4. Read the reset flow end to end, including how the email link is built.
  5. List every API key type. Find the middleware. Check what "valid" means for each.

Five links, five afternoons, no lab, no exploit server. The bugs you find this way are the ones that get CVEs later — you're just reading them first.

I'm collecting these patterns — each link anchored to real, patched public CVEs — into Auditing Open-Components: A Practitioner's Field Guide, an early-access book about auditing deployed open-source middleware from source alone.

title: How password-locking a file really works (and a 650-line tool that does it)
summary:
Argon2id turns a password into a key that is slow to guess on GPUs; XChaCha20-Poly1305 seals the file so any change is detected. This post walks through the format of skull-locker, an open-source file locker, and the one rule that keeps your original safe: never delete it until the locked copy has been opened and checked.

The rest: the README's "Why another file locker" table and the "Use" section, then a link to https://github.com/skull-org/skull-locker.

title: I built a tiny programming language for Halloween — then made property tests prove it behaves
summary:
This post is part of Kiroween 2026 — it's the story of my Skeleton Crew entry, CurseEngine.

The idea started with a grumble: every automation tool I rely on asks me to trust rules I can't read. Moderation bots, reminder workflows, digest jobs — the rule fires on real people, and the person accountable for it gets a settings page, not a sentence.

So I built the opposite. CurseEngine is a small language where a rule is one line of near-English:

curse spam-strikes: when message where count(message by same author flagged) >= 3 within 7 days -> mute author for 1 day; escalate to owner

A hand-written parser compiles that to an inspectable graph. A sandboxed executor runs it — no eval, no LLM making the call. And because a rule you can't rehearse is still a gamble, the same executor doubles as a simulator: run it over history and see what would have happened, with zero side effects. Every real action lands in an append-only log — the grimoire — where undo appends a reversal instead of erasing history.

One engine, three hosts: GrimMod (chat moderation — a raid bot muted on its third flagged message), Deadbeat (invoice chasing at 7/14/21 days, exactly once per tier), and a standup-digest rule-pack. After the engine's baseline commit, the apps were added with zero changes to the engine package. That diff is the whole Skeleton Crew argument, and it's checkable in the git history.

The part I did not expect: the property-based tests found the best bug. The suite runs 1,500 generated event streams through the live executor and the simulator and demands identical outcomes. On the first run it shrank a disagreement about stacked mutes down to a tiny example — a wrong assumption that my hand-written tests shared, which is exactly why they would never have caught it. The generators are wider now (hostile regex patterns, wrong-typed fields, webhook and timer curses), and the parity count is asserted inside the test so it can't silently shrink.

The build itself was spec-first in Kiro: four specs, steering files with three inviolables (no exfiltration, the simulator never executes side effects, every action is reversible), and a hook that re-runs the whole property suite every time a curse or fixture is saved — a hook I trust because we deliberately broke a fixture once and watched it fail. Total agent cost: about 50 of the 4,000 hackathon credits. Writing the decisions down turned out to be the cheap part's best friend.

Try it live: GrimMod and Deadbeat are both running (links in the repo), and the code is MIT at github.com/pintu544/curseengine. If you run a small community or chase invoices solo, I'd genuinely like to know which curse you'd write first.

title: Why fnmatchcase Matters for Cross-Platform Python Tools
summary:
In toml-sort, a configuration override for servers.Beta could also apply to servers.beta on Windows. On Linux, it didn't.

The input file and configuration were identical. The difference came from Python's fnmatch.fnmatch(), which toml-sort used to match TOML key paths.

An Override That Shouldn't Match

toml-sort lets you override sorting options for individual TOML tables. For example, this configuration enables key sorting globally but disables it for servers.Beta:

[tool.tomlsort]
sort_table_keys = true

[tool.tomlsort.overrides."servers.Beta"]
table_keys = false

Now consider a table whose name differs only in case:

[servers.beta]
z = 1
a = 2

TOML keys are case-sensitive. The override for servers.Beta shouldn't apply to servers.beta, so the keys should be sorted:

[servers.beta]
a = 2
z = 1

With toml-sort 0.25.0, the original order could remain unchanged on Windows because the override matched despite the case difference. On Linux, the keys were sorted.

This could also affect toml-sort --check: the same file and configuration might pass the check on one platform and fail on another.

How fnmatch() Caused the Difference

Python's fnmatch.fnmatch() supports shell-style wildcard matching. Before matching, it passes both the input string and pattern through os.path.normcase().

On Windows, normcase() converts uppercase characters to lowercase. On Linux, it leaves the case unchanged.

For example:

import fnmatch

fnmatch.fnmatch("servers.beta", "servers.Beta")

This returns True on Windows and False on Linux.

That behavior is documented, but toml-sort wasn't matching filenames. It was matching dotted TOML key paths, whose case-sensitivity shouldn't depend on the operating system.

The relevant code was in _find_config_override().

It first looked for an exact match:

path_string = ".".join(path)

if path_string in self.sort_config_overrides:
    return self.sort_config_overrides.get(path_string)

If that failed, it tried the configured patterns:

matches = [
    config
    for pattern, config in self.sort_config_overrides.items()
    if fnmatch.fnmatch(path_string, pattern)
]

The exact lookup was already case-sensitive. The fallback wasn't consistently so.

Even servers.Beta, which contains no wildcard, could match servers.beta through that fallback on Windows.

The fix in PR #110 changed one function call:

- if fnmatch.fnmatch(path_string, pattern)
+ if fnmatch.fnmatchcase(path_string, pattern)

Unlike fnmatch(), fnmatchcase() doesn't normalize the strings through os.path.normcase(). It performs case-sensitive matching regardless of the host platform.

Wildcard support and the existing exact-match priority were preserved.

The fix was released in toml-sort 0.26.0 on November 14, 2026.

Reproducing Windows Matching on Linux

The regression test needed to catch a Windows-specific problem even when running on Linux.

A normal case-sensitivity test on Linux wouldn't have done that. The original fnmatch() call already behaved correctly there.

Instead, the test uses ntpath, Python's Windows-oriented path module, together with pytest's monkeypatch fixture:

import ntpath
import os

monkeypatch.setattr(os.path, "normcase", ntpath.normcase)

This replaces the normalization function used by fnmatch() with the Windows implementation.

With the original code, patterns that differ only in case can now match on Linux as they would on Windows. The updated fnmatchcase() call is unaffected.

The upstream test covers five patterns against the TOML path servers.beta:

Pattern Expected match
servers.beta Yes
servers.* Yes
servers.Beta No
Servers.* No
servers.[A-Z]* No

The last case checks a case difference inside a character class, rather than ordinary text.

The test also checks toml-sort's sorting behavior. It creates a small TOML document with unsorted keys and supplies an override that disables sorting when the pattern matches.

If the pattern should match, the keys must remain in their original order. Otherwise, they must be sorted.

Before the fix, the simulated Windows normalization made the three case-mismatched patterns select the wrong override. With fnmatchcase(), all five expectations are satisfied.

The test doesn't emulate an entire Windows environment. It replaces the specific normalization step responsible for this bug.

That makes the platform-dependent failure visible to Linux CI without needing a Windows runner for this particular check.

Matching the Data, Not the Platform

fnmatch() isn't inherently the wrong function. Its platform-dependent normalization can be useful when that's the intended matching behavior.

For TOML identifiers, however, it introduced a dependency on the operating system that the format itself doesn't have.

In this case, switching to fnmatchcase() made override selection consistent, and the regression test checked that consistency through the resulting sorting behavior.

  • toml-sort repository
  • PR #110 — Match TOML override patterns case-sensitively
  • Original implementation (v0.25.0)
  • Fixed implementation (v0.26.0)
  • Python documentation — fnmatch
  • TOML v1.0.0 specification
  • toml-sort on PyPI
